html:
A boom in wild rubber from the Amazon rainforest, from about 1879 to 1912, when the Amazon was the world's main source of rubber. Rubber had been used by the peoples of the Americas for thousands of years, as in the Mesoamerican ballgame; Goodyear's vulcanising process of 1839 made it useful for industry, and bicycles and then cars wanted tyres.

The latex came from wild trees scattered through the forest. Tappers, many of them migrants fleeing drought in northeastern Brazil, worked in debt to traders. In the upper Amazon, firms such as the Peruvian Amazon Company enslaved Indigenous people. The Putumayo atrocities they committed were exposed by Roger Casement, as he had exposed those in the Congo. Tens of thousands died.

Manaus and Belém grew rich, with electric streetcars and the famous Manaus opera house. The boom ended when plantations in British Malaya and Asia, grown from seeds smuggled out of Brazil in 1876, produced rubber far more cheaply. Wild rubber prices collapsed after 1912.
